ART 505: UI Design: Styling and Prototyping introduces students to the theory and practice of user interface design, focusing on visual communication tools and skills to facilitate prototyping.
Students will acquire a knowledge of the UI design thinking process, centering on the user's visual experience, which is crucial to how users interact with an interface.
Students will learn how to collaborate as a visual designer in creating interactive screen-based interfaces for websites and apps, creating visual components while considering their interactive properties, look and feel, responsiveness and interactivity and recognizing the multiple human factors, audiences and contexts that govern their design decisions.
ART 506: UI Motion Design introduces motion design in user experience within a framework of the three foundational principles of communication, orientation, and correlation.
Students will learn how motion design can complement visual affordances to provide users with more meaningful experiences and interactions.
It explores motion design as a sequence of movements that affects the user’s perception of any interface a user interacts with.

ART 507: UI Icon Design introduces and develops the skills needed to conceptualize and design icons for user interfaces.
The context, design and application of UI icons will be critiqued based on the effectiveness and appropriateness of the design language.
Students will learn to generate UI icon sets through a process that explores visual rhetoric and shape form creation through a logical visual process.
This course provides an overview of the nature and purpose of icons in user interfaces, their key characteristics, and aesthetic rules commonly used in websites and apps.

The Faculty Senate Executive Committee found no evidence that the Faculty Senate ever rescinded the missing Policy, gave an informational report on this matter to the Faculty Senate on October 19, 2023, and reposted a link to the policy in Appendix G along with a brief explanation about what had occurred.

Additional changes aim to 1) accurately reflect the relationship between academic policies and collective bargaining agreements and state and federal statutes and regulations, 2) clarify the nature of the University Manual as the official policy document where policies are not only described but also codified through legislative processes, and 3) correct an error in fact (it is not the President of the Faculty Senate, but rather the entire body of the Faculty Senate that has the authority to jointly own policies).

GEC End-of-Year Report for the May 7, 2026, Faculty Senate Meeting General Education Assessment: C2 and D1 Outcomes This is a summary of the key findings and recommendations from the General Education assessment, focusing on the C2—Global Responsibilities—and D1—Integrate and Apply—outcomes.
Starting with C2: the expectation is that all students reach competency by graduation.
The outcome is designed to position students within a global framework by asking them to engage with histories, cultures, institutions, and languages, and to move beyond understanding toward identifying and analyzing responsible action in response to complex global issues.
In principle, it’s one of the most ambitious components of the GenEd program: it aims to cultivate knowledge and foster a sense of ethical responsibility and purpose within an interconnected world.
Among the most urgent ﬁndings, which is echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proﬁciency in a language other than English among our students.
This isn’t a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

What we see in the data is partial progress toward that goal.
Most students place at the level of approaching competency , with stronger performance in applying regional knowledge, understanding global systems, and reflecting on their own cultural perspective.
These are important strengths that suggest our curriculum is building foundational global awareness effectively.
However, there are consistent gaps.
Students struggle most with communicating in a language other than English, considering multiple perspectives, and—most notably—examining global responsibilities.
Even at the upper levels, where we see developmental gains, these areas remain underdeveloped.
The data suggest that students are better at knowing than at doing —that is, they can describe global issues but are less prepared to engage them critically or propose solutions.
We also note a structural limitation: only about 37% of courses participated in the C2 assessment.
That level of participation constrains how broadly we can generalize these findings.

Turning to D1: this outcome is intended to move students beyond disciplinary silos by emphasizing the interconnectedness of knowledge and its application to complex, real-world problems.
Positioned primarily at the 300- and 400-level, it assumes that students will draw on prior learning across the GenEd curriculum to synthesize ideas, transfer skills, and respond eﬀectively to new academic and professional challenges.
In

this sense, D1 represents the culminating logic of GenEds: not just the accumulation of knowledge, but its integration and use.
Here the results are stronger.
Students most often meet or approach competency, particularly in transferring skills, connecting knowledge, and engaging in integrative learning.
This is encouraging and suggests that, where integration is explicitly built into coursework, students perform well.
That said, the D1 data come with even more significant limitations.
Only 13% of courses participated, and the sample is heavily weighted toward upper-division courses, limiting representation of earlier stages in the undergraduate experience and our ability to assess developmental progression.
So, while the results are positive, they are not yet comprehensive.
Across both outcomes, student performance is closely tied to assignment design.
Where assignments are well aligned with GenEd outcomes, students demonstrate competency.
Where that alignment is unclear—or where assignments do not explicitly ask for reflection, perspective-taking, or application—student performance drops accordingly.

So, what’s next? ● First, GEC recommends clearer and more explicit guidelines for aligning assignments with GenEd outcomes, particularly in Kuali submissions. ● Second, we recommend investment in faculty development—workshops and resources that help instructors design assignments that elicit the kinds of learning we are trying to measure. ● Third, and critically, we need to find a way to increase faculty participation in assessment.
Without broader participation, we risk turning assessment into a compliance exercise rather than a meaningful tool for program improvement. ● Finally, we recommend that certain criteria be revisited—especially––and I emphasize this: language use within C2, to see how criteria are defined and implemented across disciplines, to ensure they are both rigorous and applicable.
A Key Emerging Concern: Language Proficiency Among the most urgent ﬁndings echoed in both assessment data and anticipated student feedback, is the persistently low level of proﬁciency in a language other than English among our students.
This isn't a marginal issue; it represents a structural weakness in the current GenEd framework.

At a time when we position global competency, intercultural awareness, and cross-cultural communication as central institutional goals, the fact that relatively few students graduate with functional proﬁciency in another language reveals a misalignment between our stated outcomes and our curricular realities. We're asking students to demonstrate global understanding without consistently providing them the most fundamental tool required to achieve it. This raises a set of unavoidable questions for the committee and for the university: What is the role of language study within General Education? And more importantly, can we credibly claim to prepare students for global citizenship and an increasingly multilingual workforce if language proﬁciency remains peripheral to the curriculum? Without sustained and meaningful engagement in language learning, our claims of intercultural competence risk remaining aspirational rather than demonstrable. If C2 is to function as more than a conceptual framework, then we need to treat language proﬁciency as a central pathway to achieving its goals, not as an optional enrichment. Despite our stated goals of fostering global understanding and communication across cultures, relatively few students graduate with functional proficiency in another language. This disconnect raises fundamental questions about: ● The role of language study within our GenEd requirements ● Whether GenEd is adequately preparing students for global citizenship and workforce demands In short, the program is working, but unevenly. Students are learning, but not always in the ways we intend to measure. With stronger alignment, clearer expectations, and broader participation, we can close that gap.

General Education Advisory Committee Final Report 2024-2025-1 Committee Membership The committee’s roster for the 2024-2025 school year was: ● Joëlle Rollo-Koster, A&S Chair ● Sen. Jay Fogleman (2027), COE ● Rachel DiCioccio, OIGE ● Elaine Finan, ATL ● Christian Gonzales, A&S ● Shane Tutwiler, COE ● Amanda Missimer, CHS ● Prasasti Pandit, A&S ● Daniel Carpenter, A&S ● Robert Widel, A&S Purpose of Committee In May of 2024, the Faculty Senate approved a proposal to create a Special General Education Advisory Committee (GEAC) to assist the General Education Committee (GEC) in fulfilling its duties related to the evaluation of the General Education Program. The GEAC was to receive specific guidance from the GEC, and present its recommendation regarding the need for a similar committee beyond the 2024-2025 year. Executive Summary The GEAC was formed in response to a proposal in the Faculty Senate for a special committee to assist the GEC in evaluating the General Education program (GEP). The committee reviewed three sets of General Education Learning Outcomes Assessment Data Runs for the 2021, 2022, 2023 assessment efforts and contributed to the corresponding Outcomes Assessment Reports. The committee met monthly to discuss these results and recommendations. The committee’s findings point to encouraging signs of student competency in most areas, but also highlight critical challenges, particularly in low faculty participation and alignment of assessment practices. The GEAC strongly affirms that sustained improvement in GEP will hinge on a more engaged and better-supported faculty, clearer alignment between assignments and assessment tools, and a commitment to equity in the evaluation process. 1

Based on its work, the GEAC recommends that a standing advisory body similar to this committee be continued beyond the 2024–2025 academic year to ensure ongoing reflection, responsiveness, and renewal of the GEP.
Constitute a Committee of General Education Stakeholders The GEAC was formed in August 2024 for the purpose of reviewing General Education Outcome Data and making recommendations for enhancing the GEP.
The committee was convened by the GEC Chair, Jay Fogleman.
Invited committee members included a variety of GE stakeholders, a representative of the ATL Assessment Office, the Director of the Office of Innovation in General Education, an assessment methodologist, as well as several faculty recognized as effective and experienced General Education instructors.
The GEAC met monthly in the fall to review and discuss existing outcomes evaluation data.
Joëlle Rollo-Koster, A&S, was appointed as committee Chair by the committee in the first meeting.
The process of convening and charging the GEAC was presented to the FSEC in mid September of 2024.

Review Existing General Education Outcome Evaluation Data and Make Recommendations The committee summarized the data and made recommendations for program improvement.
Committee members were charged with reviewing outcome data provided by the Outcomes Office and providing recommendations.
Committee feedback was collected and organized around broad areas of improvement.
The committee chair used this feedback and meeting discussions to complete the results and recommendation sections on the outcomes reports for the four of the six outcomes based on committee discussions and feedback (2021, 2022).
The GEC chair completed similar work for the last two outcomes for the 2023 report.
The GEC chair consolidated the GEAC feedback and kept the GEC informed of the progress of the GEAC and integrated their concerns into GEAC discussions.
Outcomes Assessment Results Year (Spring) Outcomes Examined Number of Artifacts Collected Number of Artifacts Scored Faculty Participation (Act/Poss) * 100 Overall Average Competency Notes 2021 B2 - Communicate Effectively 661 36 22/71 31% 1.63/3 (Approaching) 2021 B4 - Information Literacy 1454 139 56/179 31% 1.92/3 (Approaching) 2

2022 B1 - Write Effectively 639 60 39/169 23% 2.49/3 (Competent) 2022 C1 - Civic Knowledge and Responsibility 827 84 59/108 54% 2.10 (competent) 2023 B3 - Math, Stat, Comp Literacy 451 144 32/85 38% 2.43 (competent) 2023 C3 - Diversity and Inclusion 649 52 14/89 16% 2.27 (competent) Key Findings ● Faculty participation rates for all of the outcome assessments were low, ranging from 16% to 51%.
Despite the low response rate, results from samples for all outcome assessments were deemed generalizable. ● Generally, students are competent with four of the outcomes, approaching competency on the remaining two outcomes. ● A significant number of submitted student artifacts were not accessible, mainly due to not being de-identifiable.
Recommendations The GEAC reviewed evaluation data for six of the General Education outcomes and has identified several key areas to enhance faculty participation in and assessment of the General Education program.
To increase faculty participation in the evaluation process, the committee emphasizes the need for structured support systems, regular professional development, and alignment of assignments with rubrics.

Additionally, it highlights the importance of incentivizing faculty through recognition in tenure and promotion processes.
The committee also recommends periodic review of outcomes and targeted training for all faculty involved in General Education courses.
Evaluation processes should be refined to ensure assessments prioritize questions that can inform program improvement, document student growth over time, and include student voice in the process to better understand how students value their general education.
These recommendations aim to foster a more engaged and committed faculty, improve the quality of General Education courses, and ensure meaningful and equitable assessment practices.
Increase Faculty Awareness, Engagement and Participation ● Implement resources to support faculty involvement in the General Education program. 3

● Strengthen faculty identity and engagement through regular training and professional development. ● Recognize participation in the assessment process in tenure and promotion processes. ● Support faculty understanding and buy-in of outcomes targeted for assessment: ● Communicate early with instructors of outcomes to be evaluated to determine potential assessments. ● Conduct virtual open forums to align rubrics and assignments for assessed outcomes. ● Review and align assignment templates with rubrics to facilitate faculty participation.
Refine Assessment Practices: ● Use the initial round of assessments as a baseline and support faculty in developing a plan to prioritize, support, and measure improvements in coming years. ● Periodically review outcomes, rubrics, and assessment tools for potential improvements. ● Ensure sufficient assessment of marginalized students to determine their standing relative to outcomes. ● Focus on realistic expectations of student competency and lifelong learning.

Conclusion and Plans for 2025-2026 The General Education Advisory Committee (GEAC) has fulfilled its charge for the 2024–2025 academic year by providing a detailed review of outcome evaluation data and offering concrete recommendations to strengthen the assessment and delivery of General Education.
The committee’s findings point to encouraging signs of student competency in most areas, but also highlight critical challenges, particularly in faculty participation and alignment of assessment practices.
Faculty needs to be more engaged.
On the other hand, in this current climate it is difficult considering that general education is taking a hit at most institutions.
The GEAC strongly affirms that sustained improvement in the GEP will hinge on a more engaged and better-supported faculty, clearer alignment between assignments and assessment tools, and a commitment to equity in the evaluation process.
Closer collaboration between the GEC and the Office of Innovation in General Education would strengthen the faculty’s voice and ownership in the development of the GEP over time.

Based on its work, the GEAC recommends that a standing advisory body of this nature be continued beyond the 2024–2025 academic year.
Such a committee can serve as a vital bridge between faculty, administration, and the GEC, ensuring ongoing reflection, responsiveness, and renewal of the GEP. 4

Powers and Duties of Committees FACULTY SENATE - December 7, 2023 Context:Several committee chairs and/or members of standing Faculty Senate committees have invisible duties that are not clearly specified in the By-Laws, especially the additional joint committees on which chairs automatically serve.
These proposed changes aim to clarify all invisible duties of Faculty Senate standing committees.

Existing language: 4.40 The Committee for Research and Creative Activities (henceforth referred to as the “full committee”) shall consist of faculty and students active, experienced, or concerned with various aspects of research, creative, and scholarly efforts at URI.
The full committee shall serve as the representative voice of the university community in all matters related to research, creative, and scholarly activities and shall seek to improve the environment for research at URI in all ways possible.
The full committee shall also comprise two subcommittees, theCompetitive Grants Subcommittee and the Center Review Subcommittee.

Each subcommittee shall comprise three faculty members serving on the full committee and three or more additional Senators appointed on a staggered basis.
The chairs of the subcommittees shall be appointed from the members of the full committee.

University of Rhode Island Faculty Senate INITIAL REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON TECHNOLOGY AND INFRASTRUCTURE

The CTI’s Goals and Objectives for AY 23-24: Overall Goal: Continue collaboration with Information Technology Services and review and make policy recommendations regarding the implications on academic and research planning, standards, services, physical facilities, and allocation of resources on all matters pertaining to information technology, infrastructure, computing, communications, and networking. Primary objectives for AY 23-24: • Ensure protection of academic freedom in all matters related to IT. • Advocate for all faculty’s teaching and research needs to be met in all matters related to IT.
